p1af: A lot of people get stuck right here. You call up the Nurturer (which can already feel a bit awkward) and try to talk to your little one, and the answer you hoped for doesn't come. Maybe just silence, or a numb feeling, or some voice saying this is silly. And all of a sudden your phone, or dinner, or the clothes still sitting in the washer feel really urgent.
p1bf: A lot of people get stuck right here. You call up the Nurturer and try to talk to your little one, and instead of the answer you hoped for, you get silence, or numbness, or some voice saying "this is silly." And all of a sudden your phone, or dinner, or some small chore around the house feels urgent. Sometimes your hand is already on the phone before you notice.
p1cf: A lot of people get stuck right here: you call up the Nurturer, try to talk to your little one, and you don't get the answer you hoped for. Maybe it's just silence, or you don't feel much of anything, or there's a voice saying, "This is silly." That last one can sound really convincing. And all of a sudden your phone feels urgent, or dinner, or some small chore around the house.
p4a2: Before you started building the Nurturer, Protector and Guide, you already had a way of treating yourself, learned from how people treated you growing up: the parent you inherited. It can be warm, but for a lot of people it starts out as a critic or a warden with rules like don't cry, don't be needy, don't get angry, don't embarrass us, don't get too independent. That's the inherited critic voice, though it doesn't always talk (sometimes it's feelings, expectations or habits). To keep belonging, your little one learned which feelings and needs to put out of sight.
p5c2: The parent you inherited also measures whatever you show the world against an impossible ideal, and then attacks you from both sides: you're not good enough, and anything that does look good is fake anyway. That second one doesn't even make sense, but it's one place feeling fake can come from. When a new grown-up voice shows up saying "Trust me," of course your little one doesn't answer.
p5b2: That critic also holds up whatever you show the world against an impossible ideal, then attacks from both sides: you're not good enough, and anything that looks good is fake anyway. The second one is one place feeling fake can come from, and it can hit even when something is actually going well. Now a new grown-up voice shows up saying "Trust me," and of course your little one doesn't answer.
p6c3: I don't blame them. The new voice doesn't have to win your little one over on the first day, and it doesn't have to start inside you either. It can be a person who likes you the way you are, a plan you wrote down when you were calmer, or one concrete thing you do to protect them. It earns their trust by showing up again and again while they watch from wherever they're hiding.
ag2: Get as close to it as you really can right now, and bring your little one in with you. They might go numb, or just say "Bullshit." That becomes the conversation, and it's worth listening to. If you pour more spirituality on top instead, none of it is getting to them.

Pick one thing to do that's small enough to repeat. A big gesture you later drop would only prove them right to doubt you, but a small thing you keep doing can change their mind.
ldw13_14:
Your little one has their own version of that last question: "Big fuckity whoopty doo. What are you gonna do for me?" They actually want to know, though I think the first answer may be that you keep loving them, even while they don't believe you. What you do for them takes days to add up, but the moment they doubt you, you can show them right away that the love stays and doesn't turn into an accusation. Then their trust can grow from the stuff back in "Not Every Hero Wears A Cape," like hearing out the sarcasm, or finally opening that envelope.

If your stomach tightens while your little one waits for an answer, slower exhales may help you stay with them. Feeling calmer doesn't mean their complaint is wrong, though, and it won't make them trust you on its own.
askgod_sec:
### Ask God for a Loan

The dog kind of love is real love. Some people also know a love that's a whole different size, like God's, or whatever opened up for them in prayer or on a long retreat, and I don't want to lump that in with the dog. If you've been there, don't shrink it down to a thought experiment about a friend.

Get as close to it as you really can right now, and bring your little one in with you. They might go numb, or just say "Bullshit." That becomes the conversation, and it's worth listening to. If you pour more spirituality on top instead, none of it is getting to them.
vow_sec16:
## Make a Simple Vow

If your promises still mean something to your little one, maybe because you've kept a few small ones, a quiet vow can help too. As many real-life parents know, your heart really explodes in such an unexpected and wonderful way when you hold your newborn baby for the first time (happened to me!). And if you're not yet a parent, it can really help to imagine holding a baby in your arms to make the vow feel real. Imagine you just had a baby, how would you feel? Would you look at him/her with adoration and joy? Carry that into visualizing yourself with your own inner child:

> "I know you're in there. I love you. You don't have to love me back or trust me yet. I can't promise that nothing painful will happen. Or that I'll always know what to do, or never react badly. But I can promise to tell you the truth and listen when you're angry. I'll make our life together safer where I can, and take the next step I can see to protect you. When I fail, I'll come back to make it right. You don't have to believe these words. Watch what I do."

Notice it only promises what you can keep, so your little one can actually watch you keep it.

Only say the "I love you" part if you can feel it. If you don't feel the love yet, say you care (with the goodwill prayer from before). That's a first step. Or even before that, just promise your little one you won't be cruel to them on purpose.

Whichever you choose, your little one may still answer with "Big fuckity whoopty doo." That's allowed, and one beautiful session wouldn't convince me either. Pick one thing to do that's small enough to repeat. A big gesture you later drop would only prove them right to doubt you, but a small thing you keep doing can change their mind.

Whenever your little one shows up looking for their parent, even if they don't know that's what they are doing, you go back to being the one they can rely on, and you're kind to them while you do it. If they show up to have some innocent fun, don't "put them in their place" as the adult. But sometimes they show up as the one who doesn't want to go to bed. Now you're in my mom's place: you still go to bed, and staying kind about it shows them bedtime isn't a lack of love.
